subject: History
source: National Curriculum KS2 (changes in Britain from the Stone Age to the Iron Age); no school Drive history material found for Y3, written from scratch

lessons.unit: Unit 1: Stone Age to Iron Age Britain
lessons.title: What was prehistory? A timeline of early Britain
objectives: Place the Stone Age, Bronze Age and Iron Age in order on a timeline

keywords.def: the time before people wrote down their history
the long period when people made tools mostly from stone
the period when people began to make tools from bronze
the period when people made tools and weapons from iron
a person who digs up and studies objects from the past

starter: What does BC stand for? (Before Christ, counting backwards)
Is 1666 a long time ago? How do you know?

teach.heading: Bismillah: before writing
bullets: Prehistory means before writing
People still lived, worked and made things
We learn from objects they left behind
teach.note: Start with bismillah and curiosity. Ask how we could find out about people who left no books. Collect ideas: bones, tools, buildings, paintings.

teach.heading: Archaeologists
bullets: Archaeologists dig carefully in the ground
They find tools, bones and pottery
These finds are called artefacts
teach.note: Show a picture of an archaeological dig. Emphasise careful recording: where an object is found matters as much as the object.

teach.heading: Three big ages
bullets: Stone Age: tools made of stone, bone and wood
Bronze Age: about 2500 BC to 800 BC
Iron Age: about 800 BC until the Romans came in AD 43
teach.note: Dates are approximate and vary by source; present them as 'about'. Misconception: all people moved from one age to the next on the same day; changes happened slowly over hundreds of years.

teach.heading: Counting BC
bullets: BC years count down towards AD 1
The bigger the BC number, the longer ago
2500 BC is earlier than 800 BC
teach.note: Draw a number line on screen. Practise: which is earlier, 3000 BC or 1000 BC? Many pupils think the smaller number is earlier.

practice: Which is earlier: 2500 BC or 800 BC?
Put in order: Iron Age, Stone Age, Bronze Age.
Name one thing an archaeologist might find.
independent: Draw a timeline and mark the Stone Age, Bronze Age and Iron Age
Add the Romans arriving in AD 43
Write two sentences explaining what prehistory means
exit: Which age came after the Bronze Age?
lessons.homework: Draw a simple picture of an object an archaeologist might find and write one sentence about what it was used for.
lessons.send: SEND/EAL: colour-coded timeline with the ages already printed so pupils drag in pictures. Stretch: explain why historians use the word about with dates.

lessons.unit: Unit 1: Stone Age to Iron Age Britain
lessons.title: Hunter-gatherers of the Stone Age
objectives: Describe how Stone Age hunter-gatherers lived
Explain how stone tools were used

keywords.def: a person who finds food by hunting animals and collecting plants
a hard stone that can be chipped into a sharp edge
moving from place to place instead of staying in one home
paintings made on cave walls by early people

starter: Which comes first: Bronze Age or Iron Age?

teach.heading: Finding food
bullets: People hunted animals such as deer
They gathered nuts, berries and roots
They fished in rivers and seas
teach.note: Begin with bismillah and gratitude for food. Ask: where do we get our food from today? Compare with hunter-gatherers who had no shops.

teach.heading: Moving with the seasons
bullets: Groups were small and nomadic
They followed herds of animals
They lived in shelters or caves
teach.note: Explain nomadic simply: no permanent home. Britain was still joined to the rest of Europe by land for much of the early Stone Age, so people could walk here.

teach.heading: Stone tools
bullets: Flint was chipped to make sharp edges
Tools included axes, scrapers and spear points
Bone and antler were used too
teach.note: Show a picture of a flint hand axe. Ask what it might be used for: cutting meat, scraping hides, chopping wood. Do not claim pupils can try making real flint tools without safe supervision.

teach.heading: Art and fire
bullets: People painted animals on cave walls
Lascaux cave in France is famous
Fire gave warmth, light and cooked food
teach.note: Lascaux paintings are around 17,000 years old. Ask what the paintings tell us about what mattered to people. Avoid saying why they painted them as fact; historians are not certain.

practice: Name two ways Stone Age people found food.
Why did hunter-gatherers move from place to place?
independent: Draw a day in the life of a Stone Age family with labels
Write three sentences using the words nomadic, flint and hunter-gatherer
Choose: would you prefer to be a Stone Age hunter or a modern shopper? Give one reason
exit: Why were Stone Age people nomadic?
Which material was used to make sharp tools?
lessons.homework: List five foods you eat and say which of them a Stone Age person could have found without farming.
lessons.send: SEND/EAL: picture word bank and sentence stems 'Stone Age people used ... to ...'. Stretch: explain one problem with finding food only by hunting and gathering.

lessons.unit: Unit 1: Stone Age to Iron Age Britain
lessons.title: The Neolithic revolution: farming and Skara Brae
objectives: Explain why farming changed how people lived
Describe what Skara Brae tells us about Stone Age homes

keywords.def: the New Stone Age, when farming began in Britain
growing crops and keeping animals for food
a place where people build homes and live
a Stone Age village on Orkney in Scotland

starter: Name two ways hunter-gatherers got food.
Which age comes before the Bronze Age?

teach.heading: A big change: farming
bullets: Farming reached Britain about 6,000 years ago
People grew wheat and barley
They kept cows, sheep and pigs
teach.note: Bismillah. Explain that farming arrived in Britain around 4000 BC. Use 'about'. Ask: what is the advantage of growing food in one place?

teach.heading: Staying in one place
bullets: Farmers needed to stay near their crops
They built permanent homes
Villages and tools for farming appeared
teach.note: Contrast nomadic hunter-gatherers with settled farmers. Ask pupils what they would need if they stayed in one place: shelter, storage, tools.

teach.heading: Skara Brae
bullets: Skara Brae is on Orkney, Scotland
It was built about 5,000 years ago
Houses were made from stone slabs
teach.note: Skara Brae was lived in from about 3180 BC to 2500 BC. A storm in 1850 uncovered it. Show pictures of stone beds, dressers and a central hearth.

teach.heading: What stone furniture tells us
bullets: Beds and shelves were made of stone
Each house had a central fireplace
Tools and jewellery were found there
teach.note: Ask: what clues show people stayed there for a long time? Accept answers about furniture and storage. Misconception: stone furniture was uncomfortable; beds had heather and skins on top.

practice: How did farming change where people lived?
Why was stone used to build at Skara Brae?
Name one thing found in a Skara Brae house.
independent: Draw the inside of a Skara Brae house and label four features
Make a Venn diagram: hunter-gatherers, farmers, both
Write a paragraph beginning 'Farming changed life because ...'
exit: Name two crops grown by Neolithic farmers.
What does Skara Brae show us about Stone Age life?
lessons.homework: Design a Neolithic house: draw it and list three features it would need.
lessons.send: SEND/EAL: pre-labelled picture of the house with a word bank. Stretch: suggest why Orkney had few trees and what that means for building materials.

lessons.unit: Unit 1: Stone Age to Iron Age Britain
lessons.title: Stonehenge, the Bronze Age and the Iron Age
objectives: Describe what Stonehenge is and when it was built
Explain how bronze and iron changed tools and life in Britain

keywords.def: a prehistoric circle of standing stones in Wiltshire
a metal made by mixing copper and tin
a hard metal used to make strong tools and weapons
a settlement on a hill protected by banks and ditches

starter: Why did farming mean people stayed in one place?
Which came first: Stone Age or Iron Age?

teach.heading: Stonehenge
bullets: Stonehenge is in Wiltshire, England
Building began about 5,000 years ago
It was built in stages over many hundreds of years
teach.note: Start Stonehenge about 3000 BC with the earthwork; the large stones came later, about 2500 BC. Show a diagram of the circle. Historians do not know for certain why it was built: say 'ideas include'.

teach.heading: Moving huge stones
bullets: Some stones came from Wales
Large sarsen stones came from near Marlborough
People had no wheels or metal tools to help
teach.note: The smaller bluestones came from the Preseli Hills in Wales, roughly 150 miles away. Ask how people might have moved them; teamwork, ropes, sledges and rollers are ideas, not certain facts.

teach.heading: The Bronze Age
bullets: Bronze is copper mixed with tin
Bronze tools and jewellery were made
Trade brought metals to Britain
teach.note: Show bronze axe heads. Explain that tin was rare so trading was important. Ask: why is bronze better than stone for some jobs?

teach.heading: The Iron Age
bullets: Iron was stronger and cheaper than bronze
People lived in roundhouses and hillforts
Tribes such as the Celts farmed and traded
teach.note: Show a roundhouse reconstruction and Maiden Castle hillfort. Mention the Iron Age lasted until the Romans arrived in AD 43. Use 'tribes' rather than claiming all were one group.

practice: Why was it hard to move the stones?
Name one use for bronze and one for iron.
independent: Write a short fact file on Stonehenge with four facts
Draw an Iron Age roundhouse and a hillfort, adding labels
Complete a table showing Stone Age, Bronze Age and Iron Age tools
exit: Which metal is made by mixing copper and tin?
Give one reason people built hillforts.
lessons.homework: Research Stonehenge or a hillfort and write three facts in your own words.
lessons.send: SEND/EAL: fact file template with sentence starters. Stretch: explain why historians are careful when saying why Stonehenge was built.
